title: Exploit Protection
summary: Exploit protection is the family of host and process hardening features that make memory-corruption and similar software flaws harder to turn into reliable code execution. It is implemented through operating system mitigations that are compiled into binaries and enforced at load time, including address space layout randomisation, data execution prevention, control-flow integrity and control-flow guard, stack and heap integrity checks, structured exception handling overwrite protection, and arbitrary code guard, alongside runtime exploit protection settings that can be applied per process through platform tooling. In practice a security team defines a baseline of mitigations, audits which production binaries and third-party agents opt out, and remediates the opt-outs through vendor updates or configuration. The control raises the cost of vulnerability exploitation and, critically, causes attacks that depend on predictable memory layouts or writable executable regions to fail outright or to crash the target process, which generates high-value telemetry. It addresses exploitation of public-facing applications, client-side exploitation, and privilege escalation that relies on memory corruption in privileged services, and it complicates process injection techniques that require executable memory in a remote process. Honest limitations matter here. Mitigations are not a patch: a logic flaw, a design weakness, or a misuse of legitimate functionality is entirely unaffected. Whole classes of modern attacks, including those abusing legitimate scripting hosts and credential access through operating system interfaces, do not touch memory corruption at all. Mitigations are frequently disabled during troubleshooting and never re-enabled, and older in-house or line-of-business binaries often cannot be rebuilt with control-flow integrity. Failure modes include system-wide opt-outs applied to make a single legacy application run, per-process exclusions that quietly accumulate, and treating a mitigation audit as a one-time project rather than a continuous control that must be re-verified after every application update.
objectives: Explain each major exploit mitigation and the specific exploitation primitive it is designed to disrupt.
Describe how to audit per-process mitigation opt-outs across a production estate and prioritise remediation.
Explain how control-flow integrity and arbitrary code guard change the feasibility of process injection and memory corruption exploitation.
Describe how exploit mitigation enforcement differs between system-wide policy and per-application configuration.
Identify the vulnerability classes that exploit protection does not address at all, and the compensating controls required.
Explain how mitigation-related crashes appear in endpoint telemetry and how to triage them as potential exploitation attempts.
Evaluate the operational tradeoffs of enforcing strict mitigation policy against legacy line-of-business software.

beginner.definition: Exploit protection is a set of built-in defences that make software flaws harder to turn into working attacks. It includes randomising where code sits in memory, marking areas as non-executable, and checking that programmes follow their intended path. When an attack breaks these rules, the programme often crashes instead of being taken over. That crash is also a useful warning.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many serious attacks depend on a bug that lets an attacker write into memory and then run their own code. These defences do not remove the bug, but they make the attacker job much harder and less reliable. Failures often show up as crashes, which gives your team something to investigate. The limits matter: these settings do nothing against weak passwords, bad permissions, or abuse of legitimate tools.
howItWorks: Operating systems apply these protections to a programme automatically when it starts.
Memory positions are randomised, so an attacker cannot rely on a fixed address.
Sections of memory are marked non-executable, so injected code cannot run there.
Checks confirm that a programme jumps only to valid, expected places in its code.
Security teams audit which programs are exempt, because opt-outs quietly weaken everything.
A crash caused by a broken rule is reviewed as a possible attack attempt.
beginner.example: Think of a warehouse where every pallet has a random location each day. A thief who studied last week layout finds nothing where it should be. Some shelves also refuse to hold anything that could be set on fire, and a guard checks that workers only walk the marked routes. A thief who trips these rules sets off an alarm instead of escaping with goods.
takeaways: Turn these defences on, then find and fix the programmes that opt out.
Treat unusual crashes on sensitive services as possible attack attempts.
Remember they do not help against stolen passwords or weak permissions.
